I hit my tool budget mid-slice, so rather than hand you a half-built archive I'll stop and report. Here's where things stand.

Where the project actually is
dump.txt is at commit 7271ebb, 302 files. Contrary to what I had in mind coming in, all fifteen §16.3 Playwright scenarios are live — Slice 15 landed scenario 12 and deleted the last [Fact(Skip)] placeholder along with PendingHarnessExtension. There are eleven fewer loose ends than I expected: no unmerged docs/_append/ files either, and docs/BUILD_PROGRESS.md is a single 5,572-line file you already appended to.

So the next step is the one BUILD_PROGRESS names four separate times: the backup/restore drill, and M6 is done.

What I found while reading the two scripts that drill would exercise
This is the useful part, and it's why the slice is worth doing properly rather than as a documentation edit.

1. scripts/restore.sh could not have completed a restore. I verified pg_restore's exit-code contract against the PostgreSQL 17 source (src/bin/pg_dump/pg_restore.c, lines 458–466): it sets exit_code = AH->n_errors ? 1 : 0, so it returns 1 whenever it ignored any error at all — which --clean --if-exists routinely does. The script runs under set -euo pipefail with web already stopped, and the compose up -d web is the line after the pg_restore. The most likely outcome of the documented recovery procedure is a database that came back and an application that stayed down, with no message saying so. This has almost certainly never been run.

2. backup.sh can leave a poison file that evicts a good backup. F-16's ledger row promises "retention prunes only after a successful new dump." True for the failing run — set -e skips the prune. But the redirect has already created the file, so a truncated dump survives as the newest .dump, and the next successful run counts it toward BACKUP_RETENTION_COUNT and prunes a real one to make room. The guarantee holds for one run and breaks on the following one.

3. grep -m1 postgres picks whichever container the engine lists first. Harmless today; actively dangerous the moment a drill exists, because a drill needs a second postgres container. A backup that dumps the scratch database would succeed, be roughly the right size, and be worthless.

4. Nothing in the tree backs up the Data Protection key ring. §15 says it "must be backed up alongside the database"; F-16's row asserts it as embodied. Both scripts only print a reminder. That is a normative rule with no mechanism — and it's the half that matters, since a database without the key ring returns every account and no enrolled authenticator.

That set is coherent enough to be one ledger finding, F-38 (F-37 is the current high-water mark).

Design decisions I settled, with the verification behind them
pg_restore -l and -d both read stdin for custom-format archives — documented, so the drill needs no container-side temp file.
DbUp's journal is schemaversions (lowercase, columns schemaversionsid/scriptname/applied), confirmed from DbUp/dbup-postgresql's PostgresqlTableJournal.cs and the PostgresqlExtensions.cs:116 default. scriptname holds the embedded resource name, so the drill can assert one journal row per migration file — a check that extends itself with every future migration.
The web container runs as root. I chased this because restoring a key ring is ownership-sensitive. mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:10.0 resolves to the Ubuntu noble/resolute variant; runtime-deps' Dockerfile creates the app user (UID 1654) but never issues USER app, and your Containerfile doesn't either. So ownership is a non-issue on both engines, and compose.yaml's :U is belt-and-braces. That's what makes the key-ring restore safe to automate rather than leave as a manual step — and it's the one thing that would have made me not ship it.
podman cp / docker cp with - streams a tar through the engine's archive API, so the key ring needs no tools inside the runtime image.
The migrations parse cleanly to 22 tables and 5 views via anchored ^CREATE TABLE|VIEW, so a schema census is reliable rather than fragile.
The slice as scoped
scripts/restore_drill.sh (new) — non-destructive, spins its own scratch postgres with no published port, and gates: archive listable → restores → 22 tables and 5 views present → one journal row per migration file → every view still resolves → row census → key ring present and non-empty. Teardown by trap. Plus full rewrites of backup.sh and restore.sh, the drill wired into ci.yml's boot-smoke job (the image and migrated database are already there, so it's nearly free), a .gitignore addition that makes O§6's "git-ignored" claim actually true, and the doc set: S§15, O§6/§8/§14, F-38, BUILD_PROGRESS, _CHANGES.md. REQUIREMENTS.md deliberately untouched — §15 already states the key-ring rule normatively, so this is a defect fix at the mechanism level, not new intent.

backup.sh is written and passes bash -n; shellcheck flags only SC2317 (info, and a false positive on the EXIT-trap body — the existing scripts pass at --severity=style, so I'll restructure it rather than add a directive). I have shellcheck 0.9.0 installed here, so everything will be linted before it goes in the archive.

Say "continue" and I'll finish the remaining scripts and docs and hand you the single .tar.gz that extracts at the repo root — full files, exact paths, explicit "Files to DELETE" section, no text-manipulation scripts. One thing to note for that delivery: scripts/restore_drill.sh is a new file, and both ci_local.sh and CI's shell-scripts gate enumerate via git ls-files '*.sh' — so it won't be linted until you git add it.

Claude reached its tool-use limit for this turn.

M6 Slice 16 — the restore drill. Extract at the repo root; eleven full files at exact paths, scripts already mode 755.

bash
tar -xzf m6-slice16-restore-drill.tar.gz -C /home/kushal/src/dotnet/myrestaurant
git add scripts/restore_drill.sh     # NOT optional — see below
Files to DELETE: none. No migration, no schema change, no package change, no ADR edit, no Program.cs, no .slnx, and no C# at all.

The git add is load-bearing: scripts/restore_drill.sh is new, and both ci_local.sh and CI's shell-scripts job enumerate via git ls-files '*.sh'. Untracked, it's silently unchecked.

The drill found four defects before it could run
restore.sh could not have completed a restore. pg_restore ran under set -e with web stopped, one line before the up -d web. pg_restore exits 1 whenever it ignored any error — exit_code = AH->n_errors ? 1 : 0, read out of the PG 17 source — and --clean --if-exists ignores errors as a matter of course. The most likely outcome of the documented procedure was a database that came back and an application that stayed down, silently.

Nothing captured the key ring. §15 required it since v1.0, O§6 listed it as step 3, and F-16's own ledger row lists it under Embodied in. Both scripts printed a reminder. Every backup ever taken from this tree restores every account and no enrolled authenticator.

A failed dump could evict a good one. A truncated file survived as the newest .dump; the next successful run counted it toward retention and pruned a real backup.

grep -m1 postgres takes the first match — fine until a drill creates a second postgres container.

One ledger row, F-38, and its "Going forward" note names the shape: four documents agreed about something no code did, so a row in the embodiment column should name something executable.

Two design points worth your eye
Gate C reads its expectations out of the migrations (22 tables, 5 views today), so a new migration extends the drill by itself — and DDL reformatted past the patterns reports that rather than passing on an empty expectation.

The key ring's write direction is safe for a checkable reason. I nearly deferred it over volume ownership. aspnet:10.0 resolves to the Ubuntu variant, whose runtime-deps Dockerfile creates app at UID 1654 and never issues USER app; your Containerfile doesn't either. The app runs as root, so podman cp can't get ownership wrong on either engine. compose.yaml's :U is belt-and-braces, not load-bearing.

Verified here / not verified
Clean at shellcheck --severity=warning and --severity=style (keeping ci.yml's claim true); ci.yml YAML-parses to four jobs, nine steps in boot-smoke; the drill's pure-bash logic exercised against your real migration files; every doc edit applied by exact-match with an assert that the anchor appears exactly once, and BUILD_PROGRESS.md's first 5,572 lines hash byte-identical to yours.

No SDK and no container engine here, so none of the three scripts has been executed. dotnet test should be unchanged at 971 / 0 / 957 / 14.

Two judgement calls flagged for veto in _CHANGES.md: REQUIREMENTS.md untouched (§15's key-ring sentence was already the contract, so this is a mechanism-level defect fix), and CI runs the drill without --strict on this first landing — every FAIL gate still blocks, but I'd rather hand you a gate that goes green than one I guessed at.

M6's checklist is now empty. The next move isn't a slice, it's a tag.
